qs.q: Trans-ovarial transmission in vector-borne diseases refers to:
o: Transmission from an infected male to a female during mating
Transmission from an infected female to offspring via eggs laid
Transmission through contact with contaminated soil surfaces and debris
Transmission between sequential nymphal developmental stages within the same species
qs.e: Trans-ovarial transmission occurs when an infected female vector passes the pathogen vertically to her eggs, resulting in infected offspring. Horizontal transmission involves other routes like mating or direct contact.

qs.q: People living in forested areas are at specific risk of which vector-borne disease?
qs.e: Loiasis (African eye worm) is transmitted by deer flies (Chrysops) which inhabit rainforests.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Vector‑borne diseases are infections transmitted by arthropods such as mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies and lice. Understanding the vector, life cycle and host response guides diagnosis, treatment and public‑health control.

sections.p: These infections arise when a pathogen completes part of its development in an arthropod vector and is then introduced into a human host during feeding or contact.
b: Common vectors: mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, triatomines, lice, fleas.
Key concepts: extrinsic incubation period (EIP) and vector competence.

sections.p: Pathogens include viruses (e.g., dengue, Zika), bacteria (e.g., Borrelia, Rickettsia), protozoa (e.g., Plasmodium, Leishmania) and helminths (e.g., filarial worms).
b: Adapted to survive in both cold‑blooded vector and warm‑blooded host.
Often have surface proteins that evade innate immunity.

sections.p: The vector acquires the pathogen during a blood meal, the pathogen undergoes development (EIP) inside the vector, then is transmitted to a new host during subsequent feeding.
b: EIP length depends on temperature; warmer climates shorten it.
Transstadial transmission (e.g., ticks) and transovarial transmission (e.g., some mosquitoes) sustain cycles.

sections.p: Clinical syndromes vary by pathogen but often present with fever, rash, organ‑specific damage or neurologic signs. Severity is staged by WHO or CDC criteria where available.
b: Dengue: dengue fever, warning signs, severe dengue.
Malaria: uncomplicated vs severe (cerebral, renal, pulmonary).
Lyme disease: early localized, early disseminated, late.

sections.p: Combine epidemiologic clues with targeted laboratory tests; when tests are unavailable, rely on clinical case definitions and response to therapy.

t.a: Rapid antigen or PCR for dengue
t.b: Confirms acute infection; positive means virus present, negative early may need repeat.

t.a: Thick and thin blood smear for malaria
t.b: Detects parasites and quantifies density; high density indicates severe disease.
Positive IgM early, IgG later; false‑negatives early require repeat after 2‑3 weeks.
Four‑fold rise in titre confirms; single low titre may be past exposure.

sections.p: Treat the specific pathogen, then provide supportive care and monitor for complications. Vector control reduces incidence and is essential in low‑resource settings.
b: Antivirals (e.g., supportive care for dengue; no specific drug).
Antimalarials (artemisinin‑based combos) chosen for rapid parasite clearance; avoid monotherapy to prevent resistance.
Doxycycline for rickettsial infections; contraindicated in pregnancy.
Supportive: fluid management, antipyretics, blood transfusion for severe anemia.

t.b: Prevents mosquito bites; reduces malaria incidence dramatically.
Applies long‑acting insecticide to walls; effective where vectors rest indoors.
Larvicidal in water bodies; safe for humans and non‑target species.
Captures adult mosquitoes for surveillance and reduction; useful where resources limit large‑scale spraying.

sections.p: Key points frequently tested in exams.
b: Define extrinsic incubation period and its impact on outbreak timing.
List three diseases transmitted transcutaneously by body lice (e.g., epidemic typhus, trench fever, relapsing fever).
Differentiate dengue warning signs from uncomplicated fever.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dengue (persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, shock).
Severe malaria (cerebral involvement, respiratory distress, renal failure).
Neurologic signs in Lyme disease (facial palsy, meningitis).

faq.q: What is the extrinsic incubation period?
faq.a: The time a pathogen needs to develop inside the vector before it can be transmitted; temperature‑dependent.

faq.q: Why are bed nets more effective than indoor spraying in some areas?
faq.a: Vectors that bite late at night rest indoors; nets provide personal protection even when spraying coverage is incomplete.

faq.q: Can a negative malaria smear rule out infection?
faq.a: Early infection may have low parasitemia; repeat smear or rapid diagnostic test if suspicion remains.
